title: 2 Kings 7:1–11
context: Samaria is under siege by Ben-hadad of Syria, and the famine has become desperate (6:24–33). The king has blamed the LORD and sent to take Elisha’s head (6:31–33). Elisha answers with the LORD’s word: by this time tomorrow, fine flour and barley will sell cheaply in the gate of Samaria (7:1). The king’s captain scoffs and is told that he will see it but not eat of it (7:2). The scene then shifts to four men with leprosy outside the gate, who decide to surrender to the Syrians and find the camp empty, because the Lord had made the Syrians hear the noise of a great army (7:6–7). After eating and hiding plunder, they recognize that keeping silent on a day of good news is wrong, and they report to the city (7:9–11). A seah was a dry measure, roughly seven liters, and a shekel was a weight of silver. Both traditions read this unit as shared ground: the LORD’s word stands, he delivers his people by his own means, and he uses unlikely messengers.

verses.text: Elisha said, “Hear the LORD’s word. The LORD says, ‘Tomorrow about this time a seah of fine flour will be sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel, in the gate of Samaria.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Into a city starving under siege, Elisha announces the LORD’s word: tomorrow flour and barley will sell for a shekel. Arminian readers note that the promise comes to a king who has just blamed the LORD (6:33), showing God’s mercy offered to the undeserving and calling for a response of trust.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the word comes entirely at God’s initiative and fixes the time precisely, “tomorrow about this time.” Deliverance rests on God’s sovereign promise, not on Israel’s merit. Shared ground: both traditions hear a gracious word of rescue that the LORD will certainly keep.

verses.text: Then the captain on whose hand the king leaned answered the man of God, and said, “Behold, if the LORD made windows in heaven, could this thing be?” He said, “Behold, you will see it with your eyes, but will not eat of it.”
verses.arminianNotes: The captain scoffs that even windows in heaven could not bring such plenty. Arminian readers see culpable unbelief: he hears God’s word through the prophet and refuses it. Elisha’s reply announces a personal consequence, showing that rejecting God’s word carries real and serious accountability.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the captain’s words as unbelief that God will judge, and they stress that God’s word does not depend on human belief to come true. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly, with God’s promise standing and the captain responsible for refusing it, as 7:17–20 will show.

verses.text: Now there were four leprous men at the entrance of the gate. They said to one another, “Why do we sit here until we die?
verses.arminianNotes: Four men with leprosy sit outside the gate, living apart from the city as the law required for such disease (compare Leviticus 13:46). Arminian readers note that the narrator turns to the most marginal people in Samaria, and that their reasoning together leads them to act rather than sit and die.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note that God chooses outcasts to be the first witnesses of his deliverance. Their question, “Why do we sit here until we die?”, sets the story in motion. Shared ground: both traditions see God’s pattern of working through the lowly and overlooked to accomplish his purposes.

verses.text: If we say, ‘We will enter into the city,’ then the famine is in the city, and we will die there. If we sit still here, we also die. Now therefore come, and let’s surrender to the army of the Syrians. If they save us alive, we will live; and if they kill us, we will only die.”
verses.arminianNotes: The lepers weigh their options: death in the city, death at the gate, or a chance of life with the Syrians. Arminian readers note the realism of their reasoning and their freedom to decide. They choose the one path that might lead to life, and the narrative honors their decision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the men act from desperation, not from knowledge of what God has done, yet their choice leads them straight to his provision. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as ordinary human deliberation that God uses, and neither treats their reasoning as heroic or as faith in itself.

verses.text: They rose up in the twilight to go to the camp of the Syrians. When they had come to the outermost part of the camp of the Syrians, behold, no man was there.
verses.arminianNotes: At twilight the lepers go to the Syrian camp and find no one there. Arminian readers note the dramatic surprise: their risky step reveals what God has already done. Human action and divine deliverance meet in the empty camp, without the lepers knowing why it is empty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s deliverance already accomplished before anyone in Israel knew it. The lepers discover rather than cause the rescue. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the moment God’s hidden work comes to light, in fulfillment of the word spoken in 7:1.

verses.text: For the Lord had made the army of the Syrians to hear the sound of chariots and the sound of horses, even the noise of a great army; and they said to one another, “Behold, the king of Israel has hired against us the kings of the Hittites and the kings of the Egyptians to attack us.”
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator explains that the Lord made the Syrians hear the sound of chariots, horses, and a great army. Arminian readers see God acting directly to rescue his people, using means that leave the Syrians to draw their own conclusions about hired Hittite and Egyptian forces.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign power over the perceptions and fears of Israel’s enemies. Without a single Israelite soldier, he routs an army. Shared ground: both traditions affirm that the deliverance is entirely the LORD’s doing and that the Syrians’ panic serves his purpose of keeping his word.

verses.text: Therefore they arose and fled in the twilight, and left their tents, their horses, and their donkeys, even the camp as it was, and fled for their life.
verses.arminianNotes: The Syrians flee in the twilight, abandoning tents, horses, donkeys, and the camp as it was. Arminian readers note the completeness of the rout and the abundance left behind, which will soon feed the city. God’s rescue is generous as well as sudden.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how the narrator stresses the totality of the flight, leaving everything in place for Israel to take. The provision promised in 7:1 is now ready. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing the LORD turning an enemy’s strength into his people’s supply.

verses.text: When these lepers came to the outermost part of the camp, they went into one tent, and ate and drank, then carried away silver, gold, and clothing and went and hid it. Then they came back, and entered into another tent and carried things from there also, and went and hid them.
verses.arminianNotes: The lepers eat, drink, and begin hiding silver, gold, and clothing. Arminian readers note the very human response of starving men suddenly surrounded by plenty. The narrative records their first impulse honestly before showing their conscience at work in the next verse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the lepers’ self-interest and see the narrator preparing for their change of mind. God’s gifts can be grasped selfishly before they are shared. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse without condemning hunger, while noting that hoarding is not the right response to God’s provision.

verses.text: Then they said to one another, “We aren’t doing right. Today is a day of good news, and we keep silent. If we wait until the morning light, punishment will overtake us. Now therefore come, let’s go and tell the king’s household.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Today is a day of good news, and we keep silent.” Arminian readers see conscience and responsibility awakened: the lepers recognize that hoarding good news while others starve is wrong. Their decision to tell the king’s household shows the moral weight of sharing what God has given.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the lepers’ words a lesson that God’s blessings are meant to be shared and that silence in the face of good news is a failure of love. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a call to share God’s deliverance with others, while not reading the lepers’ motives as purely selfless, since they also fear punishment.

verses.text: So they came and called to the city gatekeepers; and they told them, “We came to the camp of the Syrians, and, behold, there was no man there, not even a man’s voice, but the horses tied, and the donkeys tied, and the tents as they were.”
verses.arminianNotes: The lepers report to the gatekeepers that the Syrian camp is empty, with animals tied and tents standing. Arminian readers note the precise testimony of eyewitnesses. Outcasts become messengers of deliverance to the city that excluded them, which highlights God’s concern for all.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the reversal: those kept outside the city bring life to those inside it. God chooses unlikely messengers to carry his good news. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the first announcement of the LORD’s rescue, brought by people the city had overlooked.

verses.text: Then the gatekeepers called out and told it to the king’s household within.
verses.arminianNotes: The gatekeepers pass the news to the king’s household. Arminian readers note the chain of human messengers, each choosing to pass the word along. God’s deliverance reaches the palace through ordinary people faithfully reporting what they have heard.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the news now reaches the king who had blamed the LORD (6:33) and whose captain scoffed (7:2). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as moving the story toward the king’s response, with the LORD’s word about to be tested and proved true.
